analysis.one_liner: Creates federally funded personal investment accounts for newborns as a supplement to Social Security.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a floor vote: introduced with zero cosponsors, it sat in a House Ways and Means subcommittee until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give every child born on or after July 1, 2000 a personal investment account inside Social Security, seeded with a one-time $1,000 payment from the Treasury and run like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, with choices among a government securities fund, a fixed-income fund, and a stock index fund. Families could add their own money — up to $7,000 a year into the account, with a tax deduction of up to $2,000 a year per family member — and at retirement the balance would pay benefits, an annuity bought from a private insurer, or a transfer to a retirement plan. The $1,000 seed money would come from shrinking the amounts transferred to the Social Security trust funds from taxes collected on benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Children born on or after July 1, 2000 would each get a $1,000 government-funded account at birth, managed by the board that runs federal workers' retirement savings, with no fees to Wall Street fund companies on the core funds. Families with spare cash could add up to $7,000 a year and take a tax deduction of up to $2,000 a year per taxpayer, spouse, and dependent — a deduction worth most, in dollars, to households in higher tax brackets that can actually save. Spouses and former spouses get survivor-annuity and divorce-decree protections, and account holders who die leave the non-government portion of the balance to heirs. The insurance industry would gain a guaranteed new market, since the government would be required to buy annuity contracts from private companies for retirees who elect them.

how_it_helps.text: Gives every child born on or after July 1, 2000 a $1,000 starter retirement account paid for by the federal government, credited when the child gets a Social Security number.
Lets families build the account with their own contributions up to $7,000 a year, and deduct up to $2,000 a year per family member from taxable income even if they don't itemize.

Keeps investment simple and low-cost by limiting choices to a government securities fund, a fixed-income fund of things like certificates of deposit and insurance contracts, and a stock index fund, all run by the federal Thrift Savings Plan board rather than private fund companies.

Protects spouses and former spouses: a married person generally needs spousal consent to take the money as a lump sum or roll it out, court divorce decrees control the balance, and former spouses can claim survivor annuities.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury pays the $1,000 for each newborn's account, and the bill pays for it by reducing the money that would otherwise be transferred to the Social Security trust funds from income taxes collected on benefits. The new tax deduction on contributions reduces federal revenue year after year. Account holders themselves sign an acknowledgment that the government does not protect them against investment losses or guarantee a return on the fixed-income and stock funds, and once they retire their monthly Social Security benefit is paid out of their account first, with the traditional trust fund covering only what the account can't.
analysis.who_pays_short: Treasury, Social Security trust funds, account holders

drawbacks.text: Account holders bear the market risk: anyone choosing the fixed-income or stock fund must sign a form acknowledging the government does not protect them from loss and does not guarantee a return, so a bad market in the wrong years means less retirement money.

The seed accounts are financed by diverting revenue away from the Social Security trust funds — money from taxes on benefits that now shores up the guaranteed program — which slightly weakens the system the accounts sit alongside.

The $2,000-a-year tax deduction is worth the most to households that already have cash to save, so the biggest tax benefits would flow to higher-income families while low-income families get only the flat $1,000.

At retirement, monthly benefits are paid out of the personal account before the traditional trust fund pays anything, shifting program costs toward the accounts and making the guaranteed benefit depend partly on investment results.
Retirees who elect an annuity get it through a private insurance company purchased on their behalf, adding a private intermediary — and its profit margin — where the fund could have paid directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: a universal $1,000 head start on retirement savings for every child and a clean, low-cost savings vehicle, with genuine spousal protections. The costs are structural — money drained from the Social Security trust funds to pay for the seed accounts, a regressive tax deduction, market risk placed on individual savers, and a new annuity market handed to private insurers. The design is more careful than typical privatization plans (no payroll-tax diversion, government-run funds, no Wall Street fees on the core options), but it still nudges the guaranteed program toward market-dependent accounts without addressing Social Security's financing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Social Security subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Petri introduced the Retirement Security Act of 1999 on May 20, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on it the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced, and a week later to that committee's Subcommittee on Social Security.
Not a single other House member — Republican or Democrat — signed on as a cosponsor.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security was left exactly as it was, keeping the benefit-tax revenue the bill would have diverted, and private insurers never got the new government-brokered annuity market. The sponsor's proposal simply lapsed; no constituency gained anything concrete from the outcome.

for.name: Rep. Tom Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave introductory remarks on the House floor the same day, and proposed creating personal Social Security investment accounts for children born after mid-2000.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee, Subcommittee on Social Security
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bill Archer, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from its May 27, 1999 referral onward without a hearing, markup, or report, letting it die when the Congress ended.

against.name: House Members of both parties
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no visible support beyond its sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Republican, backed the bill; no Democrat and no other Republican cosponsored, and no vote was ever recorded, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill requires the government to buy annuity contracts from private companies for account holders who elect annuities, complete with bonding requirements, creating a new stream of customers and premiums funded from the public accounts. A cheaper public alternative — paying annuities directly from the government fund — was available, so the industry's gain comes from inserting itself into a public payout channel.

The fixed-income fund may hold certificates of deposit and other instruments selected by professional asset managers, giving banks and managers a role in the accounts. But the funds themselves are run by the federal Thrift Savings Plan board, so the large-scale management business stays in government hands.

The bill creates an above-the-line tax deduction of up to $2,000 a year per taxpayer, spouse, and dependent for contributions to these accounts. The benefit scales with tax brackets and the ability to save, so households with spare cash capture most of the tax value while the Treasury forgoes the revenue.
